All the free schools in this section of Grayson county are attended by children from the Choctaw nation. Teachers say they learn rapidly, and some are not disposed to thoroughly comply with the rules and school discipline.

Among the Teachers' Association mentioned is one at Dodd City to meet at different places in the county at regular intervals for the benefit of all. This association seem to have been the perfection of a uniform method of teaching, and in a more efficient manner. The closing exercises of the free schools, academies, and colleges in this section are thorough. The examinations are followed by exhibitions, the exhibitions by picnics, all at the beginning of June.⁸

PRIVATE SCHOOLS AND COLLEGES.—Before the public-school system had been established and was able to take care of the needs of primary and secondary education, this section had already developed several prosperous private schools; and because the century was almost at its end before the system was firmly established in the listed in the North Texas area, the responsibility of collegiate education in the private schools and churches during the 'eighties.

In addition to this school which is the subject of this study, other colleges in operation in Fannin County during the period were a school established as the Lawyers' Institute of collegiate rank, at Ladonia; Carlton College and the Calvert Female Institute at Ladonia; and Fulton College, for boys, at Bonham; The Walcott Institute at Honey Grove; and the McKinney College at McKinney, twenty-five miles over in Grayson County, also, the long established Austin College at that time at Sherman; and the most famous of them, here, was the widely known Kidd-Key College
